# Results

Only formatting changed; no wording, number or claim was touched. -->

## Characterization of wild barley grain nutritional value traits

The four nutritional traits were quantified in 290 *H. spontaneum* accessions across three growing seasons, and for each trait genotype BLUPs were used to estimate accession-level genotypic values while accounting for season and block effects. Partitioning the phenotypic variance into genetic, season-and-block, genotype-by-season (G×E), and residual components (Fig. 1a) showed that starch had the highest broad-sense heritability (H² = 0.474; Table 1), roughly twice that of all other traits. The genotype-by-season interaction was small to moderate for all four traits (4.5–15.2%), where β-glucan combined the largest G×E component (15.2%) with the smallest genetic fraction indicating a strong genotype-specific response across the three growing seasons. Among morphological traits, flowering time (H² = 0.747) had the highest heritability and tiller number the lowest (H² \< 0.001) indicating the respective genetic control for these traits. To further explore these trends, reaction norms were generated per genotype across seasons (Fig. 1b). Overall, results were consistent with the heritability with substantial variation between specific genotypes indicating that the G×E signature is notable for all traits.

![](../../../08_USED_creating_figures/Figure_1/Fig1.png){width="6.85in"}

**Fig. 1** Genetic architecture of grain nutritional and reference traits. **a** Variance partitioning for four nutritional and four morphological traits into genetic, season + block, genotype × environment, and residual components. **b** Per-genotype reaction norms across the three seasons for the four nutritional traits; gray lines, all accessions; colored lines, four representative trajectories

To examine whether variation in grain nutritional traits followed the environmental gradient of the collection sites, trait BLUPs were first visualized across the 29 sites ordered by ecological region (Fig. 2a). This descriptive pattern suggested that northern-derived genotypes generally had higher starch, whereas desert-derived genotypes tended to have lower starch and higher fiber and β-glucan; protein showed no clear directional trend. Among the nutritional traits, starch was strongly negatively correlated with fiber (r = −0.78; Fig. 2b) and β-glucan (r = −0.53), while fiber and β-glucan were positively correlated (r = 0.35; all *P* \< 0.001). Thus, genotypes with higher starch tended to have lower fiber and β-glucan. Protein was poorly correlated with other traits, and significant negative correlation was obtained only for protein-starch (r = −0.12, *P* \< 0.05). Among the morphological and phenological traits, starch was strongly correlated with grain weight, plant height, and flowering time, while fiber showed the exact opposite pattern. Protein was also weakly negatively correlated with grain weight (r = −0.13, *P* \< 0.05). Overall, β-glucan and protein displayed weaker, mostly negative correlations, linking grain composition directly to whole-plant resource allocation and phenology (Fig. 2c). To identify which environmental variables of the sites of origin were associated with each trait, site-mean nutritional-trait BLUPs were correlated with eight environmental variables (Fig. 2d). Starch was positively correlated with clay, precipitation, and organic carbon, and negatively correlated with sand and pH. Fiber showed the opposite pattern for clay, sand, and precipitation, while β-glucan was positively correlated with sand and electrical conductivity and negatively correlated with clay, precipitation, and organic carbon. Protein was not significantly correlated with any of the measured environmental variables. Together, these associations linked the contrasting patterns of starch versus fiber and β-glucan to gradients in soil texture and precipitation, consistent with the broader geographic pattern observed across the collection sites.

![](../../../08_USED_creating_figures/Figure_2/Fig2.png){width="6.85in"}

**Fig. 2** Ecological architecture of grain nutritional traits. **a** Centered trait BLUPs of the four nutritional traits across 29 sampling sites, ordered and colored by ecological region. **b** Pearson correlations among nutritional-trait BLUPs. **c** Pearson correlations between nutritional- and morphological-trait BLUPs. **d** Pearson correlations between site-mean nutritional-trait BLUPs and eight environmental variables; cells outlined in black are significant at *P* \< 0.05. To identify the genomic regions associated with grain nutritional traits, genome-wide association was performed for each trait using the genotype BLUPs as the phenotypic input, the first three principal components as fixed covariates to correct for population structure, and a kinship matrix as a random effect to correct for relatedness among the 290 accessions, testing 7,110,996 SNPs (Fig. 3). The genomic inflation factor was close to unity for all four traits (λ~GC~ = 0.975–1.013; Fig. 3), indicating adequate control of population structure and of genome-wide false-positive inflation. <!-- src: 01_USED_GWAS_V2_pipeline/results/00_FINAL_BLUP_3PC/02_loci_FINAL/tables/Table_analysis_parameters.tsv; λGC: 01_USED_GWAS_V2_pipeline/results/tables/lambda_table.tsv (BLUP, 3 PCs), also printed in Fig. 3 -->

Overall, 52 SNPs exceeded the genome-wide threshold and resolved into 36 loci, each defined as the lead SNP together with the contiguous block of SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with it (Fig. 3; [TODO: ESM number. Fiber was the most mappable trait, with 24 significant SNPs in 18 loci, followed by β-glucan (20 SNPs, 11 loci), starch (6 SNPs, 5 loci) and protein (2 SNPs, 2 loci). Interestingly, the number of loci did not follow heritability: starch, the most heritable nutritional trait (H² = 0.474; Table 1), yielded only five loci, whereas fiber, with about half its heritability (H² = 0.248), yielded more than three times as many. The strongest association in the study was a β-glucan peak on chromosome 2H (2H:41,996,626; −log~10~(*P*) = 7.60), and the densest β-glucan signal was a cluster of ten significant SNPs on chromosome 4H (4H:34,825,152–35,062,236), [TODO: Removed from the text on 2026-09-27 (review item 5.2): the span of the 4H beta-glucan cluster (237 kb) and the second-strongest beta-glucan peak (4H:34,858,354; -log10(P) = 7.33). On chromosome 7H (573.6 Mb), the fiber locus was contained within the starch locus, and the two lead SNPs were only 154 bp apart. On chromosome 1H, four loci fell within 1.02 Mb (329.7–330.7 Mb): a starch locus nested between two fiber loci 121 kb and 58 kb away on either side, with a third fiber locus 532 kb upstream of the nearer one. On chromosome 3H (544.0–546.5 Mb), the widest fiber locus was followed 595 kb downstream by a starch locus. In contrast, none of the β-glucan loci overlapped or neighbored a locus of another trait, and the nearest one was located 6.0 Mb away, on chromosome 3H, although β-glucan was phenotypically correlated with both starch and fiber (Fig. 2b). <!-- src: locus coordinates and gaps computed from 01_.../02_loci_FINAL/tables/Table_loci_master.tsv (fiber_L17 ⊂ starch_L05; starch_L01 between fiber_L02 [121.4 kb] and fiber_L03 [58.5 kb], fiber_L01 at 1H:329,707,484 [532.1 kb upstream of fiber_L02], whole 1H cluster 329,707,484-330,726,559 = 1,019,075 bp; fiber_L08 → starch_L03 595.3 kb; nearest β-glucan cross-trait gap betaglucan_L04 → fiber_L07 6,001 kb) -->

To search for potential candidate genes, the interval of each locus, defined by its LD span, was screened for annotated genes in the MorexV3 reference genome. Together, the 36 loci covered 7.91 Mb and contained 55 candidate genes at 15 loci, whereas the remaining 21 loci contained no annotated gene. These included the four loci that consisted of the lead SNP alone, with no other SNP in linkage disequilibrium with it. Fiber contributed most of the candidate genes (32 genes at six loci), followed by starch (10 genes at three loci), β-glucan (seven genes at four loci) and protein (six genes at two loci). Notably, the three most significant β-glucan loci, on chromosomes 2H, 4H and 3H, contained no annotated gene. None of the lead SNPs was located within a gene body. <!-- src: 03_USED_candidate_genes_around_leading_snps/results/tables/results_chapter_numbers.txt (generated 2026-09-10: 7.91 Mb, 55 genes, 15 loci with genes, 21 empty, per-trait counts, 0 lead SNPs in a gene body, 3 with a functional description; fiber_L08 12 genes; betaglucan_L02/_L05/_L04 0 genes) -->

Candidate genes were further evaluated by haplotype analysis to identify phenotypic divergence between accessions carrying contrasting alleles across haplotype groups. Gene-level haplotype analysis tested whether variation across each gene was associated with the corresponding trait (Kruskal–Wallis, Benjamini–Hochberg correction within each trait, *q* ≤ 0.05) and quantified the direction and magnitude of differences among haplotype groups, information not provided by the single-SNP tests. At the acyltransferase (*GPAT6*) the five cultivars matched the two low-fiber haplotype groups closely, at 95–98% and 88–91% of called sites, and the high-fiber group at only 39–45%, so the high-fiber wild haplotype is essentially absent from these lines. To search for a candidate gene at the tightest of the three fiber–starch co-localizations, the region around the two 7H loci was examined (Fig. 3b, d). Both loci were too narrow to contain a gene, spanning 185 bp (fiber) and 1.56 kb (starch). A single gene, *HORVU.MOREX.r3.7HG0729030*, lay immediately beside them, within 732 bp of both lead SNPs and 554 bp beyond the edge of the starch locus, and the nearest other annotated gene was 112 kb away. The gene encodes a GDSL esterase/lipase predicted to be secreted, identified at the level of the family rather than as a characterized ortholog. Members of this family act on ester bonds in the plant cell wall and cuticle. In rice, the GDSL esterase DARX1 removes acetyl groups from arabinoxylan, a major fiber polysaccharide of the cereal grain, and in tomato, GDSL1/CD1 polymerizes cutin [TODO: verify these citations in the References session - written from memory, not from PDFs in the project. Plant Cell 31:1113-1126 (rice DARX1); for tomato GDSL1/CD1, Girard A-L et al (2012) Tomato GDSL1 is required for cutin deposition in the fruit cuticle. Plant Cell 24:3119-3134, and/or Yeats TH et al (2012) The identification of cutin synthase: formation of the plant polyester cutin. Nat Chem Biol 8:609-611. In the haplotype analysis, the gene resolved into two haplotype groups over 246 of the 290 accessions, with the same grouping for both traits (Fig. 5). The haplotypes were defined by a single group of four SNPs, the three significant SNPs and a fourth in linkage disequilibrium with them (7H:573,606,282; r² = 0.44–0.54). The minority haplotype B comprised exactly the 34 accessions carrying the minor allele at both lead SNPs. It had higher fiber (*P* = 2.1 × 10⁻³, η² = 0.035, 0.54 SD; Fig. 5a) and lower starch (*P* = 1.1 × 10⁻³, η² = 0.040, 0.56 SD; Fig. 5b) than the major haplotype A (*n* = 212). Thus, a single haplotype at this gene was associated with both traits in opposite directions, matching the negative phenotypic correlation between fiber and starch (Fig. 2b). At the four SNPs that defined the haplotypes, the five elite malting cultivars carried the alleles of the low-fiber, high-starch haplotype A at every called site, and none carried those of the high-fiber, low-starch haplotype B (Fig. 5c). <!-- src: haplotypes 03_01_7H_branch_Starch_Fiber_shared_signal_explore/results/tables/mgmin3_gene_results.tsv (MGmin 3, epsilon 0.9: 1 marker group, 4 of 4 signal SNPs, 27 SNPs in window, 246 assigned / 44 unassigned, groups 212|34, fiber KW p 0.00209 eta2 0.0347 delta 0.535 SD, starch KW p 0.00107 eta2 0.0398 delta 0.559 SD; ## Ecological differentiation of grain composition

Previous studies of Israeli wild barley showed that population structure, flowering time and growth traits are organized along gradients of temperature and precipitation (Hübner et al. 2009, 2013). The present study extends this ecological differentiation to grain nutritional traits. Because the comparisons were based on genotype BLUPs from common-garden experiments, the regional patterns reflect heritable differences among source populations rather than immediate plastic responses to the environments in which the accessions were collected. The contrast between the starch-rich grain of northern genotypes and the fiber- and β-glucan-rich grain of desert genotypes followed soil texture and precipitation at the sites of origin (Fig. 2), placing the carbohydrate axis on the environmental gradient of the collection.

Physiological studies provide a plausible explanation for the direction of this pattern. Heat and drought during grain filling shorten the filling period, reduce the activity of starch-synthetic enzymes, among them the heat-sensitive soluble starch synthase, and decrease starch deposition and final grain weight (Savin and Nicolas 1996). β-glucan, in turn, combined higher values in desert genotypes with the largest genotype-by-environment component of the four traits. Temperature is known to affect the content, solubility, viscosity and molecular weight of barley β-glucan, with the direction and magnitude of the response depending on genotype, stress intensity and timing: higher growth temperatures can increase soluble β-glucan in some genotype–environment combinations, whereas severe short-term heat stress reduces it and promotes its degradation (Anker-Nilssen et al. 2008). Thus, the large G×E observed for β-glucan is consistent with previous studies. Taken together, the nutritional traits were not distributed randomly across the collection but were tightly associated with the environmental conditions of the source sites.

## A shared carbon-allocation axis for starch, fiber and β-glucan

Wild barley grain composition reveals two partly distinct biological dimensions: an independent protein axis, and a coordinated carbohydrate axis defining an inverse relationship between storage starch and the cell-wall polysaccharides, fiber and β-glucan (Corke et al. 1989). This trade-off was consistently observed across genotypes and along the north-to-desert gradient (Fig. 2), indicating that grain composition reflects the competitive allocation of a common sucrose supply within the developing endosperm. This mechanism is supported by functional evidence showing that endosperm-specific overexpression of *HvCslF6* increases β-glucan accumulation while reducing starch content (Lim et al. 2020), demonstrating that these components are governed by interconnected physiological and genetic systems. The carbohydrate axis further integrates with a broader whole-plant resource-allocation strategy linked to plant architecture and phenology: larger, later-flowering genotypes with heavier grains prioritize storage starch, whereas smaller, faster-developing plants distribute resources toward higher grain numbers and structural cell-wall material. While domestication and breeding have historically shifted cultivated barley toward the starch-rich end of this axis, with higher starch and lower protein and fiber, wild barley remains a potential source of genetic variation for enriching the crop in fiber and β-glucan [TODO: This claim rests on the literature only. Morex and Clipper were grown as cultivated checks in the same common garden but carry no NIR values in 00_THIN_Generate_Plots_For_Publication/all years barley.csv (checked 2026-09-24). Check whether cultivated-check nutritional data exist elsewhere in our own study (raw NIR exports, the calibration set, collaborators' records): if they do, the wild-vs-cultivated comparison could rest on this experiment rather than on a 1988 citation. Background: section_materials/04_discussion/NOTE_cultivated_checks_no_NIR.md]{.comment-start id="401" author="TODO"}[[(Friedman and Atsmon 1988)]]{.mark}[]{.comment-end id="401"}.

The trade-off also had a genomic counterpart. Fiber and starch loci co-localized in three regions, and these resolved at three different levels. On chromosome 7H, the two loci resolved to a single gene, and a single haplotype of this gene carried both effects, higher fiber and lower starch of similar magnitude. With the two lead SNPs only 154 bp apart and no other annotated gene within 112 kb, this pattern is more simply explained by one causal variant expressed through two correlated traits than by two linked genes. Moreover, the carriers of the minor alleles at this locus, and of the haplotype carrying both effects, came from sites across the environmental gradient of the collection, so this shared signal cannot be explained as a geographic artifact of the accessions' origin. <!-- src (item 11, 2026-09-30): 11_USED_check_low_maf_geographic_distribution_minor_allele/results/tables/T02_lead_enrichment_tests.tsv rows fiber_L17 (41 carriers, 11 sites; N/C/D/HZ1/HZ2/HZ3 = 0/5/7/7/21/1; 17.1% desert vs 15.0% of major carriers; q Desert 0.81) and starch_L05 (35 carriers, 10 sites; 0/5/7/7/14/2; 20.0% vs 18.2%; q 0.82); T04_haplotype_group_enrichment_tests.tsv GDSL haplotype B (34; 0/5/7/7/14/1; 20.6% desert vs 15.1%; q 0.67). Panel desert share 50/290 = 17%. Wording by the user, 2026-09-30 ("all environments", then "sites across the environmental gradient of the collection"): the carriers come from the coast, the desert and the three transitional zones; none from the four northern sites. TODO 403 and comment 412 removed on this item (user). --> The gene encodes a GDSL esterase/lipase rather than a starch enzyme, so its link to starch is more likely compositional than mechanistic, as a shift in the cell-wall fraction changes the share of starch in the grain in the opposite direction. On chromosome 3H, the two neighboring loci resolved to two genes, one per trait, a cutin-biosynthetic acyltransferase (*GPAT6*) for fiber and a plastid phosphate transporter (*PHT4;3*) for starch. On chromosome 1H, the region contained no gene with a known role in either trait. Thus, the carbon-allocation axis was visible at every level the data could resolve. <!-- src: allele direction 01_USED_GWAS_V2_pipeline/results/00_FINAL_BLUP_3PC/02_loci_FINAL/tables/Table_loci_master.tsv (lead_beta, minor allele; Results Ch. 2); three regions and the 154 bp lead distance Results Ch. 2; 7H gene and haplotype B (fiber +0.54 SD, starch -0.56 SD) Results Ch. 4 (03_01_7H_branch_Starch_Fiber_shared_signal_explore/results/tables/mgmin3_gene_results.tsv); 3H GPAT6 and PHT4;3 Results Ch. 3; 1H: fiber loci gene-empty (03_.../results/tables/candidate_genes.tsv), starch locus genes not presented, 1HG0049610 SH3P2-like "all too indirect" (05_.../08_USED_annotation_master/TRAIT_CANDIDACY.md), 1HG0049620 not testable. DISCUSSION_CANDIDATES items 2.9-2.13, 2.16 -->

In contrast, protein was not correlated with any of the measured environmental variables, and only weakly and negatively with grain weight (Fig. 2c, d). This pattern suggests that grain protein is governed by processes that differ from those organizing carbohydrate composition. This observation is largely supported in the literature highlighting a negative relationship between grain yield or grain weight and grain protein concentration (Simmonds 1995). This negative relationship can potentially be explained by a dilution effect, where carbohydrates accumulate faster than nitrogen during grain filling, causing protein to become a smaller proportion of total grain mass (Bogard et al. 2010). Differences between wild and cultivated barley in dry-matter accumulation, nitrogen allocation and nitrogen harvest index further demonstrated that grain protein depends on the balance between carbon deposition and nitrogen acquisition rather than on direct competition with starch alone (Corke et al. 1989). Total soil nitrogen and organic carbon at the source sites were likewise not correlated with grain protein (Fig. 2d). This separation has a practical implication, as the strong starch–fiber trade-off may not impose the same constraint on protein, and increasing fiber or β-glucan need not cause a reduction in protein. At the genomic level, none of the protein candidate genes could be tested, so the genetic control of protein remains [TODO: Check how grain protein was quantified (NIR calibration against Kjeldahl; Pintel MSc thesis) - it may help discuss the protein GWAS and gene-search results (two loci, no testable gene). Decided 2026-09-25: no measurement detail in the text for now]{.comment-start id="402" author="TODO"}unresolved in this panel[]{.comment-end id="402"}.

## Heritability and GWAS reveal different aspects of genetic architecture / [suggested: **Genetic architecture of grain composition**]{.mark}

Trait heritability poorly predicted genome-wide association mapping power. Starch, the most heritable nutritional trait, yielded only five loci, whereas protein, β-glucan and fiber, each with about half its heritability and near-identical to one another, yielded two, 11 and 18 loci, respectively. This contrast emphasizes that mapping success depends on components of the genetic architecture such as the number of alleles, their frequencies and effect sizes, and linkage disequilibrium, rather than on total genetic variation alone. <!-- 2026-09-28: the GH17 5H example sentence that the next note documents ("For example, the fiber locus on chromosome 5H illustrates how a signal only just above the genome-wide threshold produced a strong separation between haplotypes once the markers across *GH17* were analyzed together.") was deleted by the user in Word; the note is kept for the record. --> <!-- Added 2026-09-26 (user): the counterpart of the mini paper's 3H starch example (old_mini_paper/md/06_discussion.md, section 3), which cannot be reused (no "marginal" class any more; PHT4;3 has a mid-range lead and the weakest effect). src: fiber_L14 lead 5H:462,564,771, -log10(P) 6.0506 vs threshold 6.0454 = the weakest fiber lead (01_.../02_loci_FINAL/tables/Table_loci_master.tsv); GH17 5HG0487060 eta2 0.222, 1.41 SD, five groups, the largest effect of the three presented genes (05_.../08_USED_annotation_master/results/tables/Table_significant_genes_paper.tsv; Results Ch. 3). The comparison is on effect size, not P: the haplotype P (2.4e-05 raw) is not smaller than the GWAS lead P. --> <!-- src: loci per trait 01_.../02_loci_FINAL/tables/Table_loci_per_trait.tsv (starch 5, protein 2, beta-glucan 11, fiber 18); H2 Table 1 (00_THIN_.../outputs/subsection_1/tables/H2_GxE.csv: starch 0.474, fiber 0.248, protein 0.242, beta-glucan 0.234); rare leads 25 of 36 with MAF < 0.10 (Table_loci_master.tsv, Results Ch. 2) -->

Most associations rested on rare alleles, and at every fiber, β-glucan and starch locus the minor allele shifted grain composition in the direction of the phenotypic correlations, toward higher fiber and β-glucan and lower starch. This consistency may partly reflect where the carriers came from: at most fiber and β-glucan loci, they originated mainly from desert and coast–desert sites, the populations that already produce low-starch, fiber- and β-glucan-rich grain ([TODO: ESM number. The carrier-origin Online Resource built from 11_USED_check_low_maf_geographic_distribution_minor_allele/results (T02 lead SNPs, T04 haplotype groups, T08 carriers vs their own site-mates - it backs the within-site sentence below, Fig_carrier_origin, Fig_desert_enrichment; ready captions in results/CAPTIONS.md); the method goes to M&M §11]{.comment-start id="419" author="TODO"}[[Online Resource X]]{.mark}[]{.comment-end id="419"}). Such regional enrichment is expected if these alleles contributed to local adaptation, and does not by itself indicate an artifact. The carriers also came from several desert sites rather than a single one, and at most loci they differed from non-carriers of their own site in the direction of the allelic effect, supporting a genetic effect beyond geographic origin. However, correction for population structure is less effective for rare alleles shared by related accessions, so a contribution of common ancestry cannot be fully excluded. Plausible gene functions further support individual loci, although the haplotypes associated with high fiber at *GPAT6* and *GH17* came mainly from several desert populations, and the high-starch haplotype of *PHT4;3* was nearly absent from them. The 7H locus, whose carriers and haplotypes were not concentrated in the desert, therefore provides the clearest case. <!-- src (item 11): 11_USED_check_low_maf_geographic_distribution_minor_allele/results/tables/T04_haplotype_group_enrichment_tests.tsv (site-permutation Desert test, BH within gene): GPAT6 group C (highest fiber) 66.7% desert vs 6.7% of the other groups, q 0.034, from 3 desert sites (Masada 6, Mount Ramon 3, Arad 3) + 2 coast-desert sites (Revivim 5, Orim 1); GH17 group C 93.8% vs 11.0%, q 0.043 (Arad 7, Maale Akrabim 7, Masada 1; Alon Hagalil 1) and group E (highest mean) 50% vs 20.6%, q 0.34 (desert: Mount Ramon 5), so the two high-fiber groups together 20 of 26 desert from 4 desert sites; PHT4;3 group A (high starch) 5.1% desert vs 39.7%, q 0.0024; GDSL haplotype B 20.6% vs 15.1%, q 0.67. ## From associated loci to candidate genes

<!-- Round 2, drafted 2026-09-26 after the user approved sections 1-3. DISCUSSION_CANDIDATES items 4.2, 4.3, 4.6, 4.9 (4.8, the population-structure paragraph with TODO 407, drafted and removed by the user 2026-09-27) (4.1 "the locus, not the gene, is the unit of discovery" is already made at the end of the rank-vs-plausibility paragraph of section 3 and is not repeated here). Parameter values (r2 0.5, 50 kb gap rule, epsilon, MGmin) stay in M&M. -->

Ranking genes by the significance of their haplotype test was a poor guide to biological candidacy. The genes with the strongest haplotype associations were often the least interpretable, unannotated or derived from mobile elements, whereas the genes with a clear route to the trait ranked lower. Because genes within a locus share one linkage-disequilibrium block, their significance largely reflects linkage with the lead signal rather than their own function. Candidate genes were therefore selected in three steps: the genome-wide association identified the locus, the haplotype test retained the genes whose variation was associated with the trait, and biological relevance chose among these genes. <!-- src: Results Ch. 3 (rank 1 6HG0619810 no functional call; rank 2 3HG0301210 transposase-derived); within fiber_L08 the two top-q genes are mobile-element-derived and within starch_L03 the top-q gene is a CRLK1-like kinase, not PHT4;3 (05_.../08_USED_annotation_master/TRAIT_CANDIDACY.md) --> The first two steps can also miss genuine candidates. The definition of loci delimits each association by linkage disequilibrium with its lead SNP, so a gene lying just outside a narrow locus is never considered. The GDSL esterase/lipase at 7H illustrates this: it lay beside two of the strongest signals of the study and was found only by examining the region directly. The haplotype analysis requires sufficient variation within a gene to define haplotype groups, so a gene that could not be tested is not a gene without effect. Likewise, one fixed grouping setting for all genes can leave the associated SNPs of a sparse gene ungrouped, so a real association can be missed even in a gene that was tested. [Refernce to the M&M]{.comment-start id="415" author="שחר לויתן" date="2026-09-28T14:28:00Z"}This was also the case at the same gene, whose associated SNPs were grouped only at a different setting (see Materials and methods).[]{.comment-end id="415"} <!-- 2026-09-27, review item 3b (user approved, with the 7H example): M&M MUST state the settings behind this: at the Ch. 3 settings (MGmin 2, epsilon 0.6) the three significant SNPs of 7HG0729030 were not grouped and the test was null (P = 0.16 fiber / 0.36 starch); the Ch. 4 result uses MGmin 3, epsilon 0.9 (03_01_7H_branch_Starch_Fiber_shared_signal_explore/README.md section 2; archive_v1_MGmin2_eps0.6/results/tables/crosshap_epsilon_sweep.tsv). --> The three genes carried forward are therefore those that passed both filters, not a complete list of the genes underlying these traits. <!-- src: locus definition (LD clumping with the lead, gap rule) 01_.../02_loci_FINAL/tables/locus_definition_params.tsv - values for M&M only; GDSL gene 554 bp beyond the starch locus, fiber and starch leads 7.25 and 6.44, the strongest of their traits (Results Ch. 4); untestable genes 25 of 55, all six protein genes (Results Ch. 3; 04_.../Stats/genes_not_tested.tsv). The "single grouping setting" sentence states the principle only; the 7H case (grouped only at a different setting) is M&M (BLUEPRINT Ch. 4, M&M hand-over) -->

[Check and verify citations]{.comment-start id="416" author="שחר לויתן" date="2026-09-28T14:30:00Z"}Each candidate gene connects its trait to a specific process in the developing grain. The acyltransferase *GPAT6* suggests that cutin deposition in the pericarp and testa contributes to the insoluble fiber fraction, consistent with the central role of GPAT6 in fruit cutin biosynthesis in tomato (Petit et al. 2016). The glucanase *GH17* suggests that the hydrolysis of cell-wall glucans contributes to grain fiber, consistent with the role of its family, which includes barley’s own (1,3;1,4)-β-glucan endohydrolases, in degrading mixed-linkage glucan (Hrmova and Fincher 2024). The phosphate transporter *PHT4;3* suggests that plastid phosphate homeostasis contributes to the metabolic conditions required for starch accumulation, consistent with the impaired grain filling reported in rice phosphate-transporter mutants (Ma et al. 2021). The GDSL esterase/lipase at 7H suggests that the modification of cell-wall esters contributes to grain fiber, consistent with the roles of this family in arabinoxylan deacetylation and cutin deposition (Zhang et al. 2019; Girard et al. 2012). Its associated SNPs <!-- 2026-09-27, review item 1.11 (user: both genes in this paragraph get a function sentence, or neither): the BS1 example (rice xylan deacetylation, Zhang et al. 2017, TODO 406) was replaced by a function sentence parallel to the PHT4;3 one. It cites the same references as Results Ch. 4 para 1 (Zhang et al. 2019; Girard et al. 2012), which are still to be verified under TODO 308. TODO 406 also noted a barley GDSL route through hull-caryopsis attachment with no citation found; it stays out of the text (section_materials/03_results/NOTE_7H_shared_signal_GDSL_gene.md). --> were confined to the putative promoter, while variants within the gene body showed no association, pointing to regulatory rather than coding variation. These four genes therefore identify distinct biological pathways for future investigation: cutin deposition, glucan hydrolysis, plastid phosphate transport and cell-wall ester modification. ## Wild alleles for cultivated barley

<!-- DISCUSSION_CANDIDATES items 6.1, 6.3 (a plain fact, not a reservation; "as expected in modern germplasm", no "malting"), 6.4, 6.5. Dropped by the user: the malting-selection reading (6.2), the desert origin of the missing alleles (6.6), the 136-line elite pool (6.7), landraces (6.8). The linkage-drag argument (Hübner and Kantar 2021) and the next steps are kept for the Conclusions. -->

The five elite cultivars shared a single haplotype at *GPAT6*, *GH17* and *PHT4;3*, as expected in modern germplasm. At *GH17* and *PHT4;3*, the cultivars carried the reference allele at every site. Since the reference genome, Morex, is itself an elite cultivar, their match with the wild groups at these genes should be interpreted with caution: at *PHT4;3* the cultivars appeared identical to the low-starch group C at the shared sites (Fig. 4f), most likely because both carry the reference allele, whereas at *GH17* they matched none of the wild groups (Fig. 4e). In contrast, *GPAT6* and the GDSL esterase/lipase, two independent loci, provided a clear result. At both genes the cultivars carried non-reference alleles at many sites, so their genotypes do not simply reflect the reference genome, and the high-fiber wild haplotype was absent from all five cultivars. At *GPAT6*, this haplotype came from three desert and two coast–desert populations rather than from a single site ([TODO: ESM number. ## Conclusions

<!-- Conclusions: drafted 2026-09-28 on S. Grain composition in wild barley is organized around carbon allocation involving starch, fiber and β-glucan, alongside a distinct protein axis governed by carbon and nitrogen balance. By applying genome-wide association and haplotype analysis to ecologically diverse populations, this research identified heritable variation and specific genetic architectures for these traits. Trait associations varied significantly and did not follow heritability; starch, the most heritable trait, mapped to few loci, whereas fiber was distributed across the most. Most associations rested on rare alleles, and β-glucan produced the strongest of them yet contributed no candidate gene. The starch–fiber trade-off recurred in the genome, most clearly at the shared 7H locus and at the neighboring fiber and starch loci on 3H, and four candidate genes link grain composition to cutin deposition, glucan hydrolysis, plastid phosphate transport and cell-wall ester modification.

These defined loci, together with the high-fiber wild haplotypes absent from the elite cultivars examined, provide precise targets for improving cultivated barley nutrition while minimizing the linkage drag commonly associated with wild germplasm introgression (Hübner and Kantar 2021). Refining broad genetic associations into a focused set of biologically plausible targets simplifies the monitoring of transferred genomic segments. Future breeding efforts must validate these haplotypes in elite cultivars, replicate their effects in independent populations, and conduct functional tests to assess their overall agronomic impact.
